subject: Biotechnology
title: How CRISPR Was Discovered
description: One-minute skill: How CRISPR Was Discovered.

hook.text: In 1987, Yoshizumi Ishino found odd repeating sequences in E. coli DNA — he had no idea what they were.

buildup.text: By 2005, researchers realized the spacers between repeats matched viral DNA — a molecular memory of past infections.

discovery.text: Bacteria store fragments of invading virus DNA — then use them as guides to find and destroy returning threats.

twist.text: The adaptive immune system everyone thought only animals had — bacteria had one all along, just different.

climax.text: Doudna and Charpentier repurposed it in 2012 — turning a bacterial defense into a universal gene editing tool.

punchline.text: A weird DNA repeat became the most powerful tool in biology.

quiz.question: What is the biological function of CRISPR in bacteria?
options: It helps bacteria reproduce faster under stress
It stores fragments of viral DNA to guide destruction of returning viruses
It produces antibiotics to kill competing bacteria

details.summary: CRISPR was discovered as a bacterial immune system where microbes store fragments of viral DNA in their genome to recognize and destroy returning invaders. Jennifer Doudna and Emmanuelle Charpentier adapted this natural system for genome editing, earning the 2020 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.
details.whyItMatters: The CRISPR discovery shows how basic research on obscure bacterial biology led to the most transformative biotechnology tool in history.
takeaways: CRISPR evolved as a bacterial adaptive immune system against viruses
Doudna and Charpentier demonstrated its use as a programmable gene editor in 2012
The discovery earned the 2020 Nobel Prize in Chemistry

faq.question: How does CRISPR function as a bacterial immune system?
faq.answer: When a bacterium survives a viral infection, it incorporates a fragment of the virus's DNA into its CRISPR array. If the same virus returns, the bacterium transcribes this fragment into guide RNA that directs Cas proteins to recognize and cut the matching viral DNA, destroying the invader.

faq.question: Who deserves credit for developing CRISPR technology?
faq.answer: The Nobel Prize went to Doudna and Charpentier for their 2012 paper demonstrating programmable DNA cutting. Francisco Mojica first identified CRISPR sequences in archaea. Feng Zhang demonstrated CRISPR editing in human cells.
